title: Rachmaninoff in exile
subtitle: The pianist, Russian scores and American studios

hero.caption: Sergei Rachmaninoff in 1925, eight years after leaving Russia. Portrait by Konstantin Somov.

intro: Rachmaninoff left Russia with his family in December 1917; by the following November he was in New York, earning his living at the piano. His records took the music of Moscow and Ivanovka into American studios, from the three notes of the C♯ minor Prelude to the short phrases of Lilacs.

stations.title: Three notes from Moscow
stations.text: The Prelude opens with three heavy notes, A–G♯–C♯, answered quietly in chords. Rachmaninoff wrote it in 1892, the year he finished his composition studies at the Moscow Conservatory, after years of training with Zverev, Siloti, Taneyev and Arensky. The following March he presented Tchaikovsky with the five piano pieces of Op. 3; the older composer especially liked the Prelude. Rachmaninoff recorded the piece for Edison in 1919. In the quiet answers the upper notes are joined into a melody above the changing chords.

cues.text: A–G♯–C♯ is played loudly; the answering chords are quiet.
The upper notes of the chords carry a continuous melody.

stations.title: The Prelude’s early circulation
stations.text: Siloti took the Prelude on his 1898 tour of Europe, England and America, and its fame travelled ahead of Rachmaninoff, who was still living in Russia. The slow opening chords give way to an Agitato in triplets, after which the three-note motif returns across the keyboard. At that point the score is written on four staves instead of two for the pianist’s two hands. A quiet coda follows, in which the chords move apart, and the piece ends softly.

cues.text: Triplets carry the melody through the Agitato.
The three-note call returns in broad chords; the printed score now stretches over four staves.
In the coda the chords are spread apart and the piano part fades to silence.

stations.title: Lilacs at Ivanovka

art.caption: Rachmaninoff stands second from the left at Ivanovka, mid-1890s. Photograph by an unknown photographer.

stations.text: Rachmaninoff wrote Lilacs in 1902 at Ivanovka, the Satin family’s estate near Tambov. In Ekaterina Beketova’s poem the speaker goes among the flowers in search of happiness. He later arranged the song as a piano piece, setting its melody among broken chords and triplets and adding short cadenzas. On 27 December 1923 he recorded that version for Victor in Camden, New Jersey. The piano part becomes quicker and fuller, pauses on a trill, then returns to the quiet melody. The final flourish adds a few more notes around the tune.

cues.text: The melody is played inside the piano’s broken chords and triplets.
The piano plays faster and louder, up to a trill held under a pause.
A short flourish leads to a soft closing chord.

stations.title: Twenty-four keys
stations.text: By 1910 twenty-three more preludes had followed the C♯ minor Prelude. The ten preludes of Op. 23 and the thirteen of Op. 32 completed Rachmaninoff’s set in all the major and minor keys. This is the B minor, played here by La Pianista in 2010. Marked Lento, it begins with small moving figures against held chords. The two hands move together in a rocking figure, then pause. The phrases gradually take on heavier chords, and the marking becomes pesante.

cues.text: Small figures rock against held chords in B minor.
The chords become heavier as the pesante passage approaches.
The broad chords begin to subside; quieter notes follow.

stations.title: December 1917: departure from Russia
stations.text: In December 1917 Rachmaninoff left Russia with his wife and two daughters. They travelled through Finland to Sweden, then settled in Copenhagen before sailing for New York in November 1918. He never saw Russia again. The B minor Prelude was already seven years old when they left. After its climax it continues with long notes surrounded by quick decoration. The opening phrases return quietly after the middle section. Near the end the bass descends and the spaces between the piano’s last sounds grow wider.

cues.text: Quick ornamental figures surround the longer held notes.
The small rocking phrases of the opening return.
The low notes and the last quiet chord die away.

stations.title: America: Edison and Victor recordings

art.caption: Konstantin Somov, Sergei Rachmaninoff, 1925: the composer during his American recording years.

stations.text: In America, Rachmaninoff worked full-time as a concert pianist. Recording became another part of that work. He recorded for Edison in 1919, signed a contract with Victor in 1920, and returned to the studio repeatedly with pieces he knew intimately. On 4 April 1928, in New York, he recorded the C♯ minor Prelude again, this time electrically. Victor issued take 23. The opening chords state the same three-note figure heard earlier, and the triplets accelerate towards the return of the opening material. The coda is quiet, as the opening was.

cues.text: Rachmaninoff recorded his Prelude again in New York on 4 April 1928, take 23.
The quiet opening gives way to the triplets of the middle section.
The opening call is played in broad chords across the keyboard.
The chords become quieter and are spaced apart as the coda begins.

stations.title: Philadelphia: the Concerto recording on shellac
stations.text: During Rachmaninoff’s treatment in Moscow in 1900, Nikolai Dahl repeated to him the promise “You will begin to write your concerto”. The Second Concerto, completed the following year, was dedicated to Dahl. In this recording, made at the Academy of Music on 10 April 1929, Rachmaninoff plays it with Stokowski and the Philadelphia Orchestra. The piano opens with bell-like chords that grow louder; the strings then take the melody while the piano plays running notes beneath them. The excerpt fills the first side of the original disc. The melody is still continuing when the side ends, at the point where a gramophone owner would have had to change the record.

cues.text: The piano begins alone with repeated chords.
The strings have the melody; the piano plays beneath them.
The piano plays a quieter phrase.
The first disc side is nearly over; the movement continues on the next record.

stations.title: Summer home on Lake Lucerne
stations.text: In the Second Concerto’s Adagio, muted strings introduce a melody for flute and clarinet above the piano’s moving notes. Rachmaninoff and Stokowski recorded this opening side in Philadelphia in 1929. Five years later, beside Lake Lucerne, Rachmaninoff was writing the Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini for piano and orchestra. Villa Senar was his summer home from 1933 to 1939. There he wrote twenty-four variations on Paganini’s last Caprice and brought in another old tune, the Dies irae. In Variation VII the piano plays that chant against fragments of Paganini’s melody.

cues.text: Muted strings open the Second Concerto’s Adagio.
Flute, then clarinet, play over the piano’s circling notes.
Piano and orchestra continue the Adagio’s long melody.
The first Adagio side ends; the song continues on another disc.

stations.title: Lilacs, revisited

art.caption: Ivanovka, mid-1890s: Rachmaninoff stands among the people of the estate where he later wrote Lilacs.

stations.text: Rachmaninoff died at home in Beverly Hills in March 1943. This recording was made twenty years earlier, in Camden: he played Lilacs. Victor’s books list twelve takes between 1920 and 1923; this is the ninth, recorded on 27 December 1923. The song’s melody passes through the moving notes, gathers into a trill and returns to a quiet close. In the photograph he is a young man at Ivanovka. On the record, a last short flourish leads to the closing chord.

cues.text: The 1923 Lilacs returns, its melody set among the moving notes.
After the trill and the quicker passage, the piano plays quietly again.
The final run ends on a quiet chord.
